subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The symbol ⇌ in an equation shows that the reaction is:
questions.explain: The ⇌ symbol indicates a reversible reaction.

questions.q: Which method could be used to measure the rate of a reaction that produces a gas?
options: Measuring the volume of gas collected over time
Measuring the colour of the flask
questions.explain: Collecting and measuring the volume of gas produced over time gives the rate.

questions.q: If the concentration of a reactant is increased in a system at equilibrium, the equilibrium shifts to:
questions.explain: Adding more reactant shifts the equilibrium towards the products to oppose the change.

questions.q: At dynamic equilibrium in a closed system:
options: All reactants have been used up
The forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate
questions.explain: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions proceed at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant.

questions.q: Increasing the pressure on a gaseous equilibrium shifts it towards:
options: The side with fewer gas molecules
The side with more gas molecules
questions.explain: Le Chatelier: higher pressure shifts equilibrium to the side with fewer gas molecules to reduce pressure.

questions.q: Adding a catalyst to a reaction at equilibrium will:
options: Shift the equilibrium to the reactants
Shift the equilibrium to the products
Reach equilibrium faster without changing the position
questions.explain: A catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but its position is unchanged.

questions.q: If the forward reaction of a reversible reaction is endothermic, what is the reverse reaction?
questions.explain: If the forward direction is endothermic, the reverse direction releases the same energy, so it is exothermic.

questions.q: At a higher temperature, a greater proportion of colliding particles:
options: Have at least the activation energy
Have less than the activation energy
questions.explain: Heating gives more particles energy equal to or above the activation energy, so more collisions succeed.

questions.q: Why is a catalyst often used in industry even though it does not increase yield?
options: It is used up so must be replaced
It gives a useful rate at lower temperatures, saving energy
questions.explain: Catalysts allow a fast enough rate at lower temperatures, reducing energy costs.

questions.q: For an exothermic forward reaction at equilibrium, increasing the temperature will:
options: Shift the equilibrium towards the reactants
Shift the equilibrium towards the products
questions.explain: Le Chatelier: raising temperature favours the endothermic direction, here the reverse (reactant) side.

questions.q: Why does a catalyst not change the amount of product made?
options: It only changes how fast equilibrium or completion is reached
It is used up in the reaction
questions.explain: A catalyst only speeds up the rate; it does not change the quantity of product formed.

questions.q: Decreasing the concentration of a product in a system at equilibrium causes the equilibrium to shift towards the:
questions.explain: Removing product makes the equilibrium shift towards the products to replace what was lost.

questions.q: On a graph of product formed against time, a steeper line shows that the reaction is:
questions.explain: A steeper gradient means more product forms per second, so the reaction is faster.

questions.q: Powdered marble reacts faster with acid than a single marble chip of the same mass because:
options: The powder has a larger surface area
questions.explain: Breaking the solid into powder exposes a larger surface area, so collisions are more frequent.

questions.q: According to collision theory, for a reaction to occur particles must collide and have at least what?
questions.explain: Particles must collide with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy to react.

questions.q: Increasing the pressure of reacting gases increases the rate because:
options: The particles are closer together so collide more frequently
questions.explain: Higher pressure squeezes gas particles closer, increasing collision frequency.

questions.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy
It increases the concentration of reactants
questions.explain: Catalysts provide an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.

questions.q: Which graph result shows that a reaction has finished?
options: The line falls back to zero
questions.explain: When no more product forms the line levels off (becomes horizontal), showing the reaction is complete.

questions.q: Lowering the temperature of a reaction decreases the rate because particles:
options: Collide less often and with less energy
questions.explain: Cooler particles move more slowly, so they collide less frequently and with less energy.

questions.q: What happens to a catalyst during a reaction?
options: It is chemically unchanged at the end
It becomes part of the product
questions.explain: A catalyst is not used up and remains chemically unchanged after the reaction.

questions.q: Which change would increase the rate of a reaction?
options: Increasing the surface area of a solid reactant
questions.explain: A larger surface area gives more sites for collisions, increasing the rate.

questions.q: How does increasing temperature increase the rate of reaction?
options: Particles move faster and collide more often with more energy
questions.explain: Higher temperature gives particles more energy, so they collide more frequently and more energetically.
